triplets.head: SDRM

triplets.head: Eaton & Gersovitz (1981)
triplets.tail: Debt with Potential Repudiation: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis

triplets.head: Eaton & Gersovitz (1981)
triplets.tail: Reputation/Exclusion Model: sovereign default is a strategic choice; countries repay because exclusion from future borrowing is costly; credit ceilings are endogenous based on borrower's income volatility

triplets.head: Bulow & Rogoff (1989a)
triplets.tail: Sovereign Debt: Is to Forgive to Forget?

triplets.head: Bulow & Rogoff (1989a)
triplets.tail: Anti-Reputation Model: reputation alone cannot sustain sovereign lending because a country can default and self-insure via foreign savings; therefore direct sanctions (trade penalties, asset seizure) are necessary

triplets.head: Bulow & Rogoff (1989b)
triplets.tail: A Constant Recontracting Model of Sovereign Debt

triplets.head: Bulow & Rogoff (1989b)
triplets.tail: Constant Recontracting/Bargaining Model: sovereign debt as continuous bargaining game; any agreement may be renegotiated; relative bargaining power determines repayment; allows for partial defaults as equilibrium outcomes

triplets.head: Tomz (2007)
triplets.tail: Reputation and International Cooperation: Sovereign Debt Across Three Centuries

triplets.head: Tomz (2007)
triplets.tail: Empirical Reputation Theory: uses 300 years of archival data from 9 countries to show reputation does sustain lending; countries ascend/descend a reputational ladder based on repayment behavior

triplets.head: Krugman (1988)
triplets.tail: Financing vs. Forgiving a Debt Overhang

triplets.head: Krugman (1988)
triplets.tail: Debt Laffer Curve: beyond a peak debt level, expected repayment to creditors falls as face value rises because default probability increases; forgiveness can make both debtor and creditors better off (Pareto improvement)

triplets.head: Sachs (1989)
triplets.tail: Conditionality, Debt Relief, and the Developing Country Debt Crisis

triplets.head: Sachs (1989)
triplets.tail: Debt Overhang as Investment Tax: large debt stock acts as tax on debtor's investment and reforms because gains flow to creditors; debt relief unlocks investment and growth, benefiting all parties

triplets.head: Calvo (1988)
triplets.tail: Servicing the Public Debt: The Role of Expectations

triplets.head: Calvo (1988)
triplets.tail: Self-Fulfilling Debt Crises / Multiple Equilibria: government debt can generate multiple equilibria where creditor expectations alone determine whether debt is sustainable; a shift in sentiment can cause default even when fundamentals support repayment

triplets.head: Cole & Kehoe (2000)
triplets.tail: Crisis Zones and Maturity Structure: DSGE model with a 'crisis zone' where both repayment and default are equilibria; longer debt maturity shrinks the crisis zone; government may optimally reduce debt to exit the zone

triplets.head: Arellano (2008)
triplets.tail: Default Risk and Income Fluctuations in Emerging Economies

triplets.head: Arellano (2008)
triplets.tail: Quantitative Eaton-Gersovitz Model: first to make the strategic default framework quantitatively operational; calibrated to Argentina matching countercyclical spreads, consumption volatility, and defaults in recessions; became the canonical workhorse model of the field

triplets.head: Aguiar & Gopinath (2006)
triplets.tail: Defaultable Debt, Interest Rates and the Current Account

triplets.head: Aguiar & Gopinath (2006)
triplets.tail: Trend Shocks Model: emerging market business cycles driven by shocks to trend growth rate (not just transitory fluctuations); worsening trend increases default incentive and current account deterioration simultaneously

triplets.head: Chatterjee & Eyigungor (2012)
triplets.tail: Long-Term Debt and Debt Dilution: extends quantitative framework to long-term bonds; new borrowing reduces value of existing bonds via dilution; maturity structure shortens as default risk rises; first to generate realistic debt levels in standard framework

triplets.head: Hatchondo & Martinez (2009)
triplets.tail: Juan Carlos Hatchondo and Leonardo Martinez

triplets.head: Hatchondo & Martinez (2009)
triplets.tail: Long-Duration Bond Modeling: introduces tractable method for modeling long-duration bonds using geometrically declining coupon structure; became a standard technical tool in subsequent sovereign default models

triplets.head: Bolton & Jeanne (2007)
triplets.tail: Structuring and Restructuring Sovereign Debt: The Role of a Bankruptcy Regime

triplets.head: Bolton & Jeanne (2007)
triplets.tail: Ex Ante vs. Ex Post Efficiency: tradeoff between making default costly (encouraging repayment) and making restructuring easy (minimizing damage); formal bankruptcy regime with seniority rules achieves better tradeoff than CACs alone; theoretical justification for SDRM-type proposals

triplets.head: Pitchford & Wright (2012)
triplets.tail: Holdouts in Sovereign Debt Restructuring: A Theory of Negotiation in a Weak Contractual Environment

triplets.head: Pitchford & Wright (2012)
triplets.tail: Holdout Bargaining Model: individual creditors hold up settlements; CACs may increase delay in complex restructurings by encouraging free riding on negotiation costs; in simple cases CACs reduce delay by >60% but in complex cases can double delay

triplets.head: Cruces & Trebesch (2013)
triplets.tail: Sovereign Defaults: The Price of Haircuts

triplets.head: Cruces & Trebesch (2013)
triplets.tail: First complete database of creditor losses (haircuts) in all 180 restructurings 1970–2010 across 68 countries; larger haircuts lead to significantly higher subsequent borrowing costs and longer capital market exclusion; overturns 'forgive and forget' consensus

triplets.head: Reinhart & Rogoff (2009)
triplets.tail: This Time is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly

triplets.head: Reinhart & Rogoff (2009)
triplets.tail: Historical Patterns across 66 countries and 800 years: serial default is the norm; countries graduate from default-prone status but can relapse; debt crises cluster with banking crises; the 'this time is different' syndrome recurs across centuries
